Module 1.title: Crystallography, Imperfections, Dislocations and Grain Boundaries
Module 1.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Crystal Structure & Defects
  • Crystal Lattices: BCC (Fe at room temp, Cr, W; APF = 0.68, CN = 8), FCC (Cu, Al, Ni, $\gamma$-Fe; APF = 0.74, CN = 12), HCP (Ti, Mg, Zn; APF = 0.74, CN = 12).
  • Atomic Packing Factor (APF): $\text{APF} = \frac{\text{Volume of atoms in unit cell}}{\text{Total unit cell volume}}$.
  • Miller Indices: Direction $[u\,v\,w]$ and Plane $(h\,k\,l)$ calculated as reciprocals of fractional intercepts.
  • Crystal Defects: Point (vacancies, interstitials, Frenkel, Schottky), Line/Dislocations (Edge: $\vec{b} \perp$ dislocation line; Screw: $\vec{b} \parallel$ dislocation line), Planar (grain boundaries, twin boundaries, stacking faults).
  • Hall-Petch Equation: Yield strength increases as grain diameter decreases: $\sigma_y = \sigma_0 + k_y d^{-1/2}$.
Module 1.detailed_notes:
Module 1 Reference: Materials Science

Dislocation motion (slip) along close-packed planes and directions constitutes the fundamental physical mechanism of plastic deformation in ductile crystalline metals.
Module 1.textbook_html:
1.1 Metallic Crystal Structures & Atomic Packing Factor (APF)

More than 90% of naturally occurring elementary metals crystallize into one of three dense periodic atomic arrangements: Face-Centered Cubic (FCC), Body-Centered Cubic (BCC), or Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP). The density of atomic packing directly determines physical ductility, density, and slip system availability.

Module 2.title: Phase Diagrams and the Iron-Carbon Equilibrium System
Module 2.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Iron-Carbon Phase Diagram
  • Gibbs Phase Rule: $F = C - P + 2$ (at constant pressure: $F = C - P + 1$).
  • Lever Rule: Phase fraction $W_\alpha = \frac{C_\beta - C_0}{C_\beta - C_\alpha}$, $W_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\beta - C_\alpha}$.
  • Three Invariant Reactions in $Fe-Fe_3C$:
    • Eutectic ($1147^\circ\text{C}$, $4.3\%\,\text{C}$): Liquid ($4.3\%\,\text{C}$) $\rightleftharpoons$ Austenite ($\gamma, 2.14\%\,\text{C}$) + Cementite ($Fe_3C, 6.67\%\,\text{C}$) [Ledeburite].
    • Eutectoid ($727^\circ\text{C}$, $0.76\%\,\text{C}$): Austenite ($\gamma, 0.76\%\,\text{C}$) $\rightleftharpoons$ Ferrite ($\alpha, 0.022\%\,\text{C}$) + Cementite ($Fe_3C, 6.67\%\,\text{C}$) [Pearlite].
    • Peritectic ($1495^\circ\text{C}$, $0.16\%\,\text{C}$): Liquid ($0.53\%\,\text{C}$) + $\delta$-ferrite ($0.09\%\,\text{C}$) $\rightleftharpoons$ Austenite ($\gamma, 0.16\%\,\text{C}$).
  • Steel vs Cast Iron: Steels: Carbon content $< 2.14\%$. Cast Irons: Carbon content $2.14\% - 6.67\%$.
Module 2.detailed_notes:
Module 2 Reference: Fe-C Equilibrium

Microstructures: Hypoeutectoid steel ($<0.76\%\,\text{C}$) contains proeutectoid ferrite + pearlite; Eutectoid steel ($0.76\%\,\text{C}$) is 100% pearlite; Hypereutectoid steel ($0.76\% - 2.14\%\,\text{C}$) contains proeutectoid cementite network + pearlite.
Module 2.textbook_html:
2.1 The Iron-Iron Carbide ($Fe-Fe_3C$) Equilibrium Phase Diagram

The Iron-Carbon phase diagram serves as the foundational map for ferrous metallurgy, heat treatment design, and alloy steel engineering. It outlines the phase transformations occurring in pure iron up to the intermetallic stoichiometric compound cementite ($Fe_3C$) containing $6.67\,\text{wt}\%\,\text{C}$.

FIG. 3.12: Iron-Carbon (Fe-Fe3C) Binary Equilibrium Phase DiagramVerified Scientific Reference

Caption: Binary phase diagram of Fe-Fe3C showing Ferrite (alpha), Austenite (gamma), Delta ferrite, Cementite, and invariant points.

Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Iron-carbon_phase_diagram.svgLicense: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0

Module 3.title: Heat Treatment of Steels and TTT/CCT Transformations
Module 3.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Heat Treatment & TTT Diagrams
  • TTT Diagram (Time-Temperature-Transformation): Isothermal transformation curve ("S-curve" or "C-curve"). Nose of the curve (approx $550^\circ\text{C}$) marks minimum incubation time for pearlite formation. Critical cooling rate (CCR) is the slowest cooling rate that avoids the nose to achieve $100\%$ martensite.
  • Key Heat Treatments:
    • Full Annealing: Heated $30 - 50^\circ\text{C}$ above $A_3$ (or $A_1$), slow furnace cooled. Produces coarse pearlite, maximum softness, and ductility.
    • Normalizing: Heated $50^\circ\text{C}$ above $A_3$ (or $A_{cm}$), still air cooled. Yields fine pearlite with higher yield strength than annealing.
    • Hardening: Heated to austenitizing temperature, water/oil quenched. Transforms FCC austenite to body-centered tetragonal (BCT) Martensite (extremely hard and brittle).
    • Tempering: Reheating quenched martensite below $A_1$ ($150 - 650^\circ\text{C}$). Relieves internal stresses, restores impact toughness via carbide precipitation.
  • Special Quenching Cycles:
    • Austempering: Quenched into salt bath above $M_s$ temperature ($250 - 400^\circ\text{C}$), held isothermally until transformation to Bainite is complete. High strength with superior toughness.
    • Martempering (Marquenching): Quenched into bath above $M_s$, equalized in temperature, then air cooled to form uniform martensite with zero quench cracking.
Module 3.detailed_notes:
Module 3 Reference: Heat Treatment

Surface Hardening Methods: Carburizing (pack, gas, liquid diffusion of carbon into low carbon steel surface), Nitriding (nitrogen diffusion forming hard alloy nitrides at $500^\circ\text{C}$ without quenching distortion), Flame & Induction Hardening.
Module 3.textbook_html:
3.1 Isothermal Transformation (TTT) Diagrams

The equilibrium phase diagram predicts phases under infinitely slow cooling rates. In industrial manufacturing, non-equilibrium cooling rates govern microstructure evolution. The Time-Temperature-Transformation (TTT) diagram maps the kinetics of isothermal austenite decomposition as a function of temperature and logarithmic time.

Caption: Time-Temperature-Transformation diagram illustrating Pearlite, Upper Bainite, Lower Bainite, and Martensite start (Ms) and finish (Mf) boundaries.

Module 4.title: Alloy Steels, Cast Irons and Non-Ferrous Engineering Alloys
Module 4.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Ferrous & Non-Ferrous Alloys
  • Alloying Elements in Steel: Cr (corrosion resistance, hardenability), Ni (toughness at low temp, stabilizes austenite), Mo (prevents temper brittleness, creep resistance), V (grain refinement), W (hot hardness for tool steels).
  • Stainless Steels: Minimum $10.5\%\,\text{Cr}$. (Ferritic: 400 series, magnetic, non-hardenable; Austenitic: 300 series e.g. 18/8 SS 304, non-magnetic, superior corrosion resistance; Martensitic: 410/420, high strength, hardenable by quenching).
  • Cast Irons: Gray CI (graphite flakes, high vibration damping, engine blocks), White CI (cementite, very hard and wear resistant), Nodular/Ductile CI (graphite spheroids via Mg/Ce inoculation, high ductility), Malleable CI (temper carbon clusters from prolonged annealing of white CI).
  • Non-Ferrous Alloys: Brass ($Cu-Zn$), Bronze ($Cu-Sn$), Duralumin ($Al - 4.5\%\,Cu - 1.5\%\,Mg - 0.6\%\,Mn$, precipitation hardenable for aircraft skins), Titanium alloys (high strength-to-weight ratio, biocompatible).
Module 4.detailed_notes:
Module 4 Reference: Engineering Alloys

High Speed Steels (HSS): 18-4-1 composition ($18\%\,W, 4\%\,Cr, 1\%\,V, 0.7\%\,C$). Retains red hardness up to $600^\circ\text{C}$ due to stable complex carbides.
Module 4.textbook_html:
4.1 Engineering Cast Irons & Microstructural Morphology

Cast irons are multicomponent ferrous alloys containing $2.14\% - 4.0\,\text{wt}\%\,\text{C}$ and $1.0\% - 3.0\,\text{wt}\%\,\text{Si}$. Silicon strongly promotes graphite carbon precipitation rather than metastable cementite.

FIG. 3.14: Microstructural Morphology of Gray, Nodular and Malleable Cast IronsVerified Scientific Reference

Caption: Comparative optical metallography showing graphite flakes in gray iron, spherical nodules in ductile iron, and temper carbon aggregates in malleable iron.

Module 5.title: Composites, Polymers, Fracture Mechanics, Fatigue and Creep
Module 5.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Fracture, Fatigue & Composites
  • Rule of Mixtures (Composites):
    • Iso-strain (Longitudinal, Voigt): $E_c = E_f V_f + E_m V_m$.
    • Iso-stress (Transverse, Reuss): $\frac{1}{E_c} = \frac{V_f}{E_f} + \frac{V_m}{E_m}$.
  • Griffith's Theory of Brittle Fracture: Fracture stress $\sigma_f = \sqrt{\frac{2 E \gamma_s}{\pi a}}$. Stress intensity factor $K_I = Y \sigma \sqrt{\pi a}$. Fracture occurs when $K_I \ge K_{Ic}$ (plane strain fracture toughness).
  • Fatigue (S-N Curve): Failure under cyclic stress below yield strength. Endurance limit (fatigue limit $\sigma_e$) is stress level below which material survives infinite cycles ($> 10^7$ cycles, present in steels, absent in aluminium).
  • Creep: Time-dependent plastic deformation under constant load at elevated temperatures ($T > 0.4 T_m$). Three stages: Primary (transient), Secondary (steady-state $\dot{\epsilon} = \text{const}$), Tertiary (accelerated rupture).
Module 5.detailed_notes:
Module 5 Reference: Failure Analysis

Fatigue design criteria: Goodman equation $\frac{\sigma_a}{\sigma_e} + \frac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_u} = 1$, Soderberg equation $\frac{\sigma_a}{\sigma_e} + \frac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_y} = 1$.
Module 5.textbook_html:
5.1 Fracture Mechanics & Griffith's Energy Balance Criterion

Linear Elastic Fracture Mechanics (LEFM) assumes that all engineering materials contain pre-existing microcracks. A.A. Griffith formulated that crack propagation occurs when the elastic strain energy released during crack advance equals or exceeds the surface energy required to create new crack fracture surfaces.
